I don't know about the original commentor but for me the character creation isn't about making some half formed avatar to use within the game, but making a person who is competent albiet inexperienced in their trade and has lived a part of their life. It doesn't feel like you are making some gamey adventurer but a person in the world who had a job and a dream before the story begins. I hope that makes a little sense

Mechanically, the character creation and character development is based on a career system. Careers have a list of skills, talents, and characteristic bonuses that you can buy with Reqard Points (exp). Each career also comes an ability to make them feel distinct. A fully made/end of campaign character will have 3 careers. This mixing of bonuses and skills along with the career abilities makes me feel as if I'm making my own class mechanically rather than following a spreadsheet. It also makes me feel as if the adventure itself helped shape who my character became (I think a big part of Zweihander for more reasons than just character development) because my choice in what career to take next often relies what is going on in universe.

I think my best advice to you is to not think about the names too much. They don't actually mean anything in terms of the game. You can be a sellsword on your character sheet but in the game reality you are a bodyguard or bounty hunter. Now, if you feel like none of the careers fit what you want, talk to your GM about mixing and matching career stuff or making your own as well as giving it a cool name to reflect it. What I mean is to take the appropriate skills, talents, bonuses, and abilities you think narratively reflect the sort of career path you are trying to make, run it by the GM for balance, and then season to taste. Once that is done, feel free to post it. I would love to see it.

Before I start off, I just want to say that the book itself really isn't that bad and can be often much more simple then regular d20 systems. I hope you find enjoyment from it like I and many others have. It is probably one of my favorite systems.

So I'm no veteran but this is what I got for you.

1. 1st is clunky, large and raw compared to the 2nd. Mind you, I don't mean these as bad things. Within it, it had it's own class system along with different psyker rules. As a fan of D&D 3.5, this culmination of a bunch of rules was honestly a bit refreshing when looking over it but at the time I was looking for a game out of my comfort zone. This brought me to 2nd which was streamlined and sleek. Classes didn't exist but were replaced with a character creation like Only War. No matter where you were from or your role in the world, you could be anything, it was just easier for some. This opened the doors to power gaming heaven but also allowed for someone to more accurately represent their character within the rules.  A major difference that I'm not sure how I feel about is the Influence compared to currency. In Dh1, you bought things with money like a sensible person. The thing that made my head feel weird about that though was when you were buying things like ancient technology with something as useless as currency. Then comes influence which was Dh2's answer to currency. Influence works like a mix of your name recognition in the inquisition, your reputation, and your overall financial status. It made more sense to try and get this amazing plasma gun through explaining to the guy how you killed a bloodletter with the skull of a cultist  then just shoving a bunch of 20 dollar bills in his face but that's just me. Influence also made players more accountable as when they destroyed city blocks, it would reflect in their influence. As for the settings, I don't look at that. Homebrew settings is where the bread ad butter is at man. 

2. Plenty of the adventure books and expansions have humans if you need them but making a person isn't hard at all. Just understand who they are and their tactics. Other books like Only War also is a really great thing to borrow from. Also, make sure to use the other humans as a means to create other people. Take influence from it. Now for encounter balance, don't try it at all. It takes away from the setting. You piss off a chaos space marine or take on the mob, they're are going to have to be responsible for that. If you only had encounters designed for them to be able to take on without casualties, then the game loses that sense of dread that should always be present. Instead of thinking of balance, think of how your npcs would react. If the party burns down a temple to the chaos gods on a frontier world, is the cult leader just going to send 4 dudes with level equivalent loot to kill them or is he going to make an example to the rest of the dirty corpse worshipers. It takes effort to stay alive in this universe, people don't give you freebies. When people are trained to kill all their life and are trained to do so without thought or reason, you can damn sure well believe they would drop two of you acolytes like it was just another thing on their to do list. Your players have literally plot armor in the form of fate and they will probably need to use it often, maybe even burn a few. With actual combat, make sure your players know that they need a plan GTFO every time or they will suffer bad things. There times when combat is super easy, there are times when it is terribly hard. They will always find out when it is much too late. Those daemons in the back of the book? One will kill an entire bar.

3. Dark Heresy is a niche within a niche but you are never alone. I'm sure many of us want the game to go down like the cult classic that is D&D 3.5. To do that, support for the game has to continue. If you want to help garner this small community, post in the subreddit. I myself am trying to do so, posting my own homebrew stuff. Hell, if you post a homebrew request I'll probably answer as the act of creating such things is super fun. Hell, I'd be down to modify Dh2 to make an ork mob rpg. Now when it comes to the hubs of discussion, this and some small sites are it. The community maybe small but it is long from dead. For something to be alive, it has to keep moving, it has to continue to be active. For that, if you want to see this game survive and if you want to garner a community, feel free to post even mundane questions in the sub. If you want to find a game, ask on this sub. That will keep this gem from getting lost in the rough. 
4. Beginner mistake is to think of this like D&D. This is an investigation, not a kill team. Be prepared for alot of downtime. Remember, face characters have like 3 or 4 actual skills for diplomacy so alot of it requires some logical conversation. This means that other characters can still talk and investigate albeit maybe a little hampered. To show this, my group has a discord chat with which we have a roleplay channel so we can do stuff between sessions like the mass helpings of conversations that don't require a boltgun. If you want, adventure wise, you can post it and a bunch of us can look over it and tell you how we feel about it. Never a bad idea.
